theme: David among the Philistines; the witch of Endor; Saul’s death
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 27:1-31:13. These chapters show David in Philistine territory, Saul’s last night, and the end of Saul’s reign. Read chapter 28 and chapter 31 with care.
settingTheScene: Weary of running, David says in his heart, “I shall be swept away one day by the hand of Saul,” and he takes refuge among the Philistines at Ziklag. Saul, meanwhile, faces the Philistine army at Gilboa with no word from God. He goes to a medium at Endor. The book ends with Saul’s defeat and death on Mount Gilboa. It is a sober ending to the story of Israel’s first king.
observation: David lives among the Philistines for a year and four months and raids the Geshurites and Amalekites (27:1-12).
Saul, afraid, inquires of the LORD, “but the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets” (28:6).
Saul disguises himself and visits the medium at Endor, though he himself had expelled mediums (28:3, 7-8).
The spirit says, “Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me” (28:19).
David returns to Ziklag to find it burned and the families taken, and “David strengthened himself in the LORD his God” (30:6).
David pursues and recovers everything, and divides the spoil fairly (30:7-25).
The Philistines defeat Israel at Gilboa; Jonathan and his brothers are killed, and Saul falls on his sword (31:1-6).
The men of Jabesh-gilead remember Saul’s rescue of their city, and recover his body (31:11-13).
interpretation:
David’s choice to live among the Philistines is a low point for him. He is tired, and his faith slips. “David said in his heart, Now I shall perish.” He does not ask the LORD. The man who has inquired of God so faithfully now decides on his own. He lies to the king of Gath and raids Israel’s enemies while pretending to raid Judah. It is a messy period, and the narrative does not hide it. Even a man after God’s own heart can have seasons of fear.

Saul’s last night is among the saddest in the Bible. God is silent. And Saul, who had banished mediums, seeks out a medium. When the spirit appears, it announces the end of his kingdom and his life. Saul falls to the ground in terror and has no strength left. He had refused to obey God when he was able, and now God does not answer. It is a picture of the cost of persistent rebellion.

Chapter 30 is the counterweight. David returns to find Ziklag burned and his wives and children captured. His own men talk of stoning him. This is his lowest moment. And here is the most important sentence: “David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.” He turns to God. He asks through the ephod, and God says, “Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue.” And so it happens.

The contrast with Saul is deliberate. Saul, in distress, consults a medium. David, in distress, strengthens himself in the LORD. Their endings differ accordingly.

Chapter 31 closes the story of Saul with a death that is tragic rather than triumphant. He dies in battle with his sons. Yet the men of Jabesh-gilead show loyalty and honor him. The book ends not with David’s triumph but with a funeral. The way to the throne is open, but it is paved with grief.
connection: Jesus was tempted to take shortcuts but trusted the Father (Matthew 4). Hebrews 3:12-13 warns against hardening our hearts in unbelief. When Jesus was alone in the garden he found his strength in prayer (Luke 22:43-44). Paul says, “Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10), and, “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).
application:
When you are discouraged, practice “strengthening yourself in the LORD.” What does that look like for you?

Think about where you turn first when you are afraid. Is it God, or something else?

Pray for someone who has hardened their heart to listen again.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what makes you afraid, and ask him to strengthen you.
Ask him to keep you from seeking answers in the dark.
Thank Jesus, who turned to the Father and never failed.
